axes.question: Was a restriction/condition/cutoff/export control actually exercised?
Did the action produce a measurable cost/shortage/industrial disruption?

axes.gap: The run closes costs and adaptation but not a specific EU political concession attributable to the exercised gas or critical-material leverage.
axes.question: Did the coercer obtain a specific requested EU political concession?

causal.counter: Uranium/VVER exposure demonstrates strategic vulnerability and precaution without an exercised Russian cutoff in this run; adaptation can occur without concession.
causal.gap: No general France/EU coercion-success denominator; no specific political concession closed for the strongest gas/critical-material cases.
causal.limit: Political success requires evidence that the target adopted the requested policy because of the coercive action; cost and adaptation are insufficient.
causal.mechanism: supplier/state -> concentrated dependency -> real control point -> deliberate restriction/condition/cutoff -> cost/disruption -> target adaptation -> requested concession or downstream effect
causal.question: When does energy or critical-material dependency become coercive leverage rather than mere vulnerability?

claims.claim: Dependency or supply concentration alone is not economic coercion.
Russia exercised a coercive gas lever against EU member states in 2022 through the ruble-payment condition and supply cutoffs/reductions.
The 2022 Russian gas reductions imposed large material costs on the EU gas/electricity system and energy-intensive industry.
The EU materially adapted through storage rules, diversification, demand reduction and progressive phaseout of Russian gas.
The Russian gas coercion caused the EU to make the requested political concession to Moscow.
claims.gap: No specific requested EU political concession is causally closed in the bounded run.

claims.claim: Chinese rare-earth/export restrictions are real control points capable of generating industrial disruption, but each episode requires separate intent and political-effect analysis.
claims.gap: Intent and political concession remain episode-specific.

claims.claim: The EU Critical Raw Materials Act is a resilience response to concentrated strategic dependencies, not proof that every dependency has already been weaponised.
Russian nuclear-fuel exposure in 2025 proves that Russia exercised an uranium/enrichment cutoff against the EU in the scoped run.
This run establishes a general prevalence or success rate of economic coercion against France/EU.

controls.control: absence of concession evidence != absence of coercive attempt

facts.subject: Russian gas dependency and weaponisation
facts.value: The Commission states that Russia attempted to weaponise Europe’s security of energy supply and that the EU had been over-dependent on one supplier for almost half of its gas imports.

facts.subject: Ruble-payment cutoff control
facts.value: Gazprom halted gas supplies to Poland and Bulgaria after they refused to pay in rubles, following a decision by the Russian President.

facts.subject: Gas weaponisation and Nord Stream reductions
facts.value: The Commission described Russia’s weaponisation of gas exports as the dominant Q3 2022 market factor and reported progressive reductions in Nord Stream 1 flows.

facts.subject: Gas price and industrial impact
facts.value: Wholesale gas prices exceeded EUR 300/MWh by end-August 2022; high prices contributed to a collapse in demand in some energy-intensive industries and to unprecedented electricity prices.

facts.subject: Flow and LNG substitution
facts.value: Russian pipeline gas imports in Q3 2022 were down 74% year-on-year, Nord Stream 1 imports down 85%, while EU LNG imports rose 89%.

facts.subject: Storage regulation adaptation
facts.value: The Council adopted rules requiring gas storage before winter, with an 80% target for 2022/23 and 90% for subsequent winters.

facts.subject: Russian gas dependency reduced
facts.value: The Commission reports Russian gas imports falling from 150 bcm in 2021 to 52 bcm in 2024, with the Russian share dropping from 45% to 19%.

facts.subject: Stepwise Russian gas phaseout
facts.value: The Council records a 2026 regulation for a stepwise prohibition of Russian gas imports and reports the Russian gas share declining from 45% in 2021 to 13% in 2025.

facts.subject: EU rare-earth dispute initiation
facts.value: The EU challenged Chinese export duties, quotas, licensing and related restrictions affecting rare earths, tungsten and molybdenum.

facts.subject: WTO rare-earth findings
facts.value: The WTO panel found challenged Chinese export restrictions inconsistent with obligations and found the export quotas served industrial-policy goals rather than the conservation justification advanced.

facts.subject: Removal after WTO ruling
facts.value: China informed the WTO that export duties, quotas and trading-right restrictions found inconsistent had been removed.

facts.subject: China 2023 critical-material export controls
facts.value: A Commission economic brief records 2023 Chinese export controls on gallium, germanium and graphite and says the gallium/germanium restrictions appear in part to react to Dutch lithography export restrictions.

facts.subject: 2025 rare-earth controls hit industry
facts.value: The IEA reports that China’s April 2025 controls on seven heavy rare earth elements sharply reduced export volumes, forcing some automakers in Europe and elsewhere to cut utilisation or temporarily halt production.

facts.subject: EU rare-earth import concentration
facts.value: Eurostat reports that China supplied 46.8% of the EU’s rare-earth imports by weight in 2025.

facts.subject: CRMA diversification architecture
facts.value: The Critical Raw Materials Act sets 2030 benchmarks of 10% EU extraction, 40% processing, 25% recycling and no more than 65% dependence on one third country, with monitoring, stress tests and strategic-stock coordination.

facts.subject: Russian uranium exposure
facts.value: In 2025 Russia supplied 15.98% of natural uranium delivered to EU utilities and 22.55% of enrichment services.

facts.subject: Nuclear stockpiling response
facts.value: Euratom reports that EU utilities have stockpiled nuclear materials and fuel since Russia’s invasion to mitigate supply-disruption risk.

facts.subject: VVER single-supplier vulnerability
facts.value: Euratom identifies dependence on a single fuel design/supplier for VVER reactors as a significant security-of-supply vulnerability and records diversification efforts.

facts.subject: Independent gas coercion corroboration
facts.value: The IEA reports that Russia attempted to impose a ruble payment system on EU buyers, leading to unilateral cuts and sanctions against certain buyers, with Russian piped exports to OECD Europe falling roughly 50% in 2022.

leads.evidence_excerpt: Trace supplier/state -> dependency -> control point -> restriction/threat/price/condition -> cost/disruption -> adaptation -> political effect.
leads.lead: Economic dependency becomes coercive leverage only when a supplier/controller deliberately restricts, conditions, threatens or interrupts a hard-to-substitute flow and the target bears measurable cost or adapts; political concession is a further edge.

leads.evidence_excerpt: Positive cases close exercised leverage and adaptation more often than a requested political concession.
leads.gap: No representative denominator and no general estimate of coercion-to-concession success rate.
leads.lead: Representative denominator for energy/critical-material dependencies converted into successful political coercion against France/EU.
